title: Weekly review
hookLine: look back on the week kindly; why the second day of creation is never called good, and what Rashi says about it
tomorrow: does a phone break the Sabbath? there's more than one answer.

lines: THE REVIEW BECOMES A LIST OF FAILURES.
GOD SAW THAT IT WAS GOOD.
DAY TWO: NO GOOD AT ALL.
cards: Sunday night, and the weekly review turns into a list of everything that went wrong. Genesis has a stranger list. Read its first chapter slowly and a refrain keeps coming back: God saw that it was good.
Day one, good. Day three, good, and then good again. Days four, five and six, good.
But the second day, when the waters are split by the firmament, gets no good at all. The rabbis noticed. Why would the maker skip a day?

teach.b: Rashi, a medieval Jewish commentator on the Torah, gives an answer. On the second day, the work of the waters wasn't finished. God divided them, but they weren't gathered into seas until the third day.
And something unfinished isn't called good yet.
So the third day gets the word twice: once for its own work, and once for finishing the second.
Then, at the end of the sixth day, comes a look over everything: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." And on the seventh day, rest.
So Genesis gives the week a shape: six days of making, a look back, and a day of rest. The Sabbath commandment in Exodus points straight back to it, and the Jewish week still ends in Shabbat.
And the look back in Genesis is generous. It doesn't pretend day two was done. It waits, and calls it good when the work is finished.
That's a kind way to review a week. Some days were good. Some are still unfinished, and unfinished is different from bad.
Their good may come on a later day. A review in this pattern isn't a trial. It's a walk back through seven days, saying good where you can, and not yet where you can't.

how: Some people keep a weekly review on Friday afternoon or Sunday evening: a quiet half hour with a notebook, walking back through each day and noting what went well, what is unfinished and what comes next.

o: a weekly score of every goal you missed
a kind look back over your week, day by day
a planning meeting for the week ahead

games.q: the first week in Genesis: tap the pairs.
p: the waters divided, no good yet

s: every day of creation in Genesis is called good
the second day isn't. Rashi says its work wasn't finished until the third.
the third day is called good twice
once for its own work, Rashi says, and once for finishing the waters of day two.
Genesis calls the finished whole very good
at the end of the sixth day: behold, it was very good.

games.q: your Sunday review: three days felt like wins; on two, the big project barely moved. what would Rashi's reading of day two say?
o: call those two days unfinished, not bad; their good may come later.
call them bad, so you're honest and push harder next week.
leave them out and review only the good days, to stay positive.
games.why: in Rashi's reading, day two isn't called good because its work wasn't done, and it gets its good on day three. unfinished isn't the same as bad.

practice: Choose your review night, Friday or Sunday, and fix it in your calendar. Then try a small one now: name one day this week you'd call good, and one you'd call not finished yet. Say both gently, the way Genesis waits for day two.

wordCard.voice: Weekly review: a kind look back over seven days, saying good where you can, and not finished yet where you can't.

orig.note: Hebrew: good. The word the refrain of Genesis 1 repeats, and leaves out on day two.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: the week, where even day two got its good in the end. See you tomorrow.
